challenges.name: commit-succeeded-publish-failed-evidence
challenges.title: DB Commit Succeeded, Publish Failed: read the evidence
challenges.description: 37 learners enrolled during a three-minute broker failover never received their welcome email, badge or certificate of enrollment. Six statements on one evidence pack - the support escalation (A), the reconciliation query (B), the service log (C), the code (D) and the broker metrics (E) - take you from the evidence to the hypothesis, past a consumer that "lost" the events and a fix that wraps the publish in the transaction, to the outbox and the test that proves it.

questions.question:
Evidence B - warehouse reconciliation, enrollments LEFT JOIN certificate receipts, per minute:
       minute        | enrolled | receipted
 2026-10-27 14:02:00 |       33 |        33
 2026-10-27 14:03:00 |       31 |        22
 2026-10-27 14:04:00 |       28 |        14
 2026-10-27 14:05:00 |       30 |        16
 2026-10-27 14:06:00 |       27 |        27

Evidence C - enrollment-service log:
14:04:12.481 INFO  POST /enrollments user=u_51207 course=postgres-performance
14:04:12.493 DEBUG tx COMMIT enrollment enr_88412 (12 ms)
14:04:17.498 WARN  publish enrollment.created failed for enr_88412: BrokerTimeoutError: publish to enrollments timed out after 5000 ms
14:04:17.499 INFO  POST /enrollments 201 Created 5018 ms
$ grep -c "WARN  publish enrollment.created failed" enrollment-service-2026-10-27.log
37      (first 14:03:13.115, last 14:05:54.310)

Statement: "The 37 learners have committed enrollment rows and their requests answered 201 Created; what is missing is only what should have happened downstream of enrollment.created."
questions.explanation: True. B counts the 37 in the enrolled column (they exist in enroll.enrollments) and only the receipts are short, by 9 + 14 + 14 = 37. C shows the order for one of them: COMMIT at 14:04:12.493, then the publish timeout, then 201 Created. So the enrollment itself is fine; the welcome email, badge and certificate, which all hang off the event, never happened. Reading this correctly matters: the repair is to emit the missing events, not to re-enroll anybody. The common mistake is to treat "the learner has no badge" as "the enrollment failed".

True. This is the dual write in order A (commit, then publish). The COMMIT is durable on its own; the publish is a second write to another system, and nothing ties the two together. During the failover the publish timed out, the catch logged a warning and returned, and the controller answered 201, so neither the learner nor any alert noticed. The 37 warnings in C match the 37 missing receipts in B. The misconception is that logging an error is handling it: after the catch, nothing remembers that the event still has to be sent.

questions.question:
Evidence E - broker dashboard and a topic search:
14:03:08  broker-2 restarted (node upgrade); leader election for partitions 1 and 4 of "enrollments"
14:05:55  all partitions of "enrollments" have a leader again
Producer errors, client enrollment-service    14:03: 9   14:04: 14   14:05: 14   14:06: 0
Records in, topic enrollments, per minute     14:02: 33  14:03: 22   14:04: 14   14:05: 16   14:06: 27
Consumer group certificate-service, max lag   14:00-14:10: 2
$ search topic "enrollments" for keys of the 37 enrollments (offsets from 14:00 to 14:10)
0 records found

Statement: "The 37 events reached the enrollments topic and the certificate consumer skipped them during the leader election; resetting the certificate-service consumer group offsets to 14:03 will deliver them."
questions.explanation: False. The topic search finds no record for any of the 37 keys, records in per minute dropped by exactly the producer error counts (9, 14, 14), and the consumer group was never more than 2 messages behind. The messages were never written, so there is nothing for the consumer to have skipped. Resetting the offsets would replay the events the certificate service already processed (deduplicated, at best) and deliver none of the 37. The misconception is to start debugging at the consumer because that is where the missing effect shows up; first check whether the message exists at all.

False. The first half is true, the second is not: the broker does not take part in the PostgreSQL transaction, so once it acknowledged the message, a failed COMMIT (serialization failure, constraint violation, crash, lost connection) cannot take it back. This is publish-then-commit, which produces ghost events, exactly the launch-day incident of lesson 1.1. It also makes every enrollment fail for as long as the broker is down (here almost three minutes) and holds the transaction open during a network call. The misconception is that anything inside the transaction callback is transactional.

False. The outbox closes the gap in the request (the event can no longer be lost or exist without its row), but the relay has its own gap: a crash, a timeout or a lost acknowledgement after the publish and before the UPDATE leaves the row pending, and the next tick publishes it again. The outbox gives at-least-once delivery. It is safe because the message id is the outbox row id, so the copy carries the same id and a consumer that deduplicates by event id processes it once. Removing the deduplication would send a second welcome email after the next relay crash. The misconception is that "transactional" on the producer side means exactly-once delivery end to end.

questions.question:
Regression test added with the outbox:

for crash of [none, "beforeCommit", "afterCommit", "afterPublish", "beforeMarkSent"]:
  for brokerDown of [false, true]:
    enroll(u1), enroll(u2) with the crash and the broker state
    restart the service; broker up; run the relay until no row is pending
    assert: each committed enrollment has exactly 1 distinct enrollment.created id
    assert: no enrollment.created exists for an enrollment that did not commit

Statement: "This test fails on the code from evidence D (at least for afterCommit and for the broker-down runs) and passes on the outbox version in every combination, which is the evidence that the dual write is gone."
questions.explanation: True. On the code from D, a crash after COMMIT or a broker outage leaves a committed enrollment with no event, so the first assertion fails; that reproduces the incident deterministically, which a log line never can. On the outbox version every combination ends with one distinct id per committed enrollment: crashes before COMMIT leave neither row, crashes after COMMIT leave a pending row the relay sends after the restart, and a crash after a publish leads to a re-publish with the same id. A test that fails on the old code and passes on the new one is the proof a fix needs; "no warnings since the deploy" only shows that no failover has happened yet.

challenges.name: commit-succeeded-publish-failed
challenges.title: DB Commit Succeeded, Publish Failed
challenges.description:
During a three-minute broker failover, 37 CodeDev learners were enrolled (their rows are committed and they got 201 Created) but the certificate service never received enrollment.created for them: no welcome email, no badge. A crash between the commit and the publish loses events the same way. The enrollment service commits the enrollment, then publishes, and swallows the publish error.

Fix createEnrollmentService so that every committed enrollment eventually produces exactly one logical enrollment.created, and no event exists for an enrollment that did not commit, whatever the broker and the process do:
- enroll(cmd) keeps its validation (409 "unknown course", "already enrolled"), writes the enrollment AND an outbox row { id: ids.next("evt"), aggregateType: "enrollment", aggregateId: <enrollment id>, eventType: "enrollment.created", payload: { enrollmentId, userId, courseId }, createdAt, status: "pending", sentAt: null } in the same db.tx(), and does not publish. Enrolling must work while the broker is down.
- relayOnce() (the scheduler calls it every second) publishes every pending outbox row, in the order the rows were written, to the "enrollments" topic as { id: <outbox id>, key: <aggregateId>, type: <eventType>, payload }, and marks a row "sent" (with sentAt) only after its publish returned. If a publish throws, leave the remaining rows pending for the next tick.
The certificate service deduplicates by message id: a row published twice with the same id counts once, a row published under two different ids counts twice.

The file provides db.tx(fn) (runs fn on a copy of the tables and commits only if fn returns), broker.publish (throws BrokerTimeout while the broker is down), ids.next(prefix) (a sequence), clock.now() and the crash points. Do not change them or the test runner.

Input (stdin, JSON): { courses: [{ id, title, seats }], steps }. A step is { op: "enroll", userId, courseId, crash? }, { op: "relay", crash? } or { op: "broker", up: boolean }. crash is "beforeCommit", "afterCommit" or "afterPublish": the process dies the first time it reaches that point during the step (every later call in that step throws Crash, even if a catch swallowed the first one), and the runner restarts the service, which loses everything held in memory.
Output: one line per enroll step with the answer ("201 Created", "409 rejected (<reason>)", "500 ..." or "no response (process crashed <point>)"), then, after a final restart with the broker up and three relay ticks, one line per committed enrollment "<userId>/<courseId>: <n> event(s)" (deduplicated by message id), the number of events that belong to no committed enrollment, and the number of outbox rows still pending. Expected: 1 event for every enrollment, 0 orphan events, 0 pending rows.
hints: After the COMMIT of enroll(), where does the information "this enrollment still needs its event" live? What happens to it when the broker is down for three minutes, or when the process is killed and restarted?

Look at the two places that touch the broker: the try/catch after db.tx() in enroll(), and relayOnce(), which does nothing today. The first must disappear from the request path; the second is where publishing belongs. In the relay, check which id goes on the wire and when a row stops being pending.

A similar case on different data: a wallet top-up writes { topup } and, in the same tx, a row { id: ids.next("msg"), kind: "wallet.credited", status: "queued" }. A worker later reads the queued rows in order, sends each one with its own row id as the message id, and only then flips it to "done" in a second tx. If the worker dies between the send and the flip, the same message id is sent again and the receiver ignores it.
